loop.name: session-task-turn-loop
loop.what: A turn is a `SessionTask` trait object spawned on a background Tokio task by `Session::start_task`, with a `CancellationToken`, a `done` Notify and an `AbortOnDropHandle`; the returned future runs to a `SessionTaskResult` and lifecycle completion is funnelled through `Session::on_task_finished` from the spawn site so every task kind shares one lifecycle. Four kinds exist (`RegularTask`, `ReviewTask`, `CompactTask`, `UserShellCommandTask`). `RegularTask::run` loops: it runs `run_turn`, and if the input queue still has pending input after the sampling round it loops again with empty input instead of ending the turn. Inside `run_turn` each iteration captures a `StepContext`, records world-state diffs, builds the sampling input, calls `run_sampling_request`, and either continues (model asked for tools / pending input), rolls over into auto-compaction on a token limit, or breaks.
invariants: Turn lifecycle terminal events must be emitted from one place: `on_task_finished` is called only by the spawn site and only when the task cancellation token was not cancelled (core/src/tasks/mod.rs:407-411).

Input tiering must be preserved: fresh turn input is sampled before pending input is drained (can_drain_pending_input starts as `input.is_empty()`), and after auto-compaction draining is re-deferred until the model no longer needs follow-up (core/src/session/turn.rs:265, :498).
A task must be `debug_assert!`-free of a second concurrent task on the same ActiveTurn: `debug_assert!(turn.task.is_none())` guards both start paths (core/src/tasks/mod.rs:341, :353).
constants: Convergence is not turn-bounded: the source comment records why an unbounded compact/continue loop is accepted — 'as long as compaction works well in getting us way below the token limit, we shouldn't worry about being in an infinite loop' (core/src/session/turn.rs:471)
Turn kinds: TaskKind::{Regular, Review, Compact} + UserShellCommandTask (core/src/tasks/mod.rs:59-64)
Per-turn OTel span attributes include model, reasoning effort and seven token-usage fields (core/src/tasks/mod.rs:367-381)

loop.name: two-tier-input-model-queue-versus-steer
loop.what: New input enters through `InputQueue`, which keeps two physically distinct paths. A *steer* is accepted only while a turn is active: `Session::steer_input` requires an active turn, rejects `TaskKind::Review` and `TaskKind::Compact` as `ActiveTurnNotSteerable`, requires a non-empty input, optionally matches `expected_turn_id` and the turn's `final_output_json_schema`, then appends into the current turn's `TurnState.pending_input` via `extend_pending_input_and_accept_mailbox_delivery_for_turn_state`. A *queued* message instead waits for the turn to end: `RegularTask::run` re-enters `run_turn` only when `input_queue.has_pending_input` reports work, and inter-agent mail sits in a separate `mailbox_pending_mails` deque behind a `watch` activity channel used as the liveness signal.
invariants: Steering must never be accepted by a Review or Compact turn, and the turn-kind match is exhaustive so a new kind forces a decision (core/src/session/turn_input.rs:507-519).
A steer may only be accepted by the turn it was addressed to; a mismatched `expected_turn_id` is rejected rather than redirected (core/src/session/turn_input.rs:498-505).

Steering must not bypass the output-schema contract: a steer whose JSON schema differs from the active turn's is rejected with `ActiveTurnOutputSchemaMismatch` (core/src/session/turn_input.rs:527-531).
constants: `NotSubmittedReason` variants include NoActiveTurn, ExpectedTurnMismatch, ActiveTurnNotSteerable, EmptyInput, ActiveTurnOutputSchemaMismatch (core/src/session/turn_input.rs:488-531)
`TurnInput` has exactly three tiers: UserInput, ResponseItem, InterAgentCommunication (core/src/session/input_queue.rs:21-30)

loop.name: idle-wake-on-pending-work
loop.what: An idle session can be woken without an explicit user turn. `maybe_start_turn_for_pending_work_with_sub_id` returns early unless the mailbox has pending items AND (some item carries `trigger_turn` OR the thread has an outstanding durable sleep registered as a `codex_extension_items::sleep::SleepItem`), then takes the active-turn lock and bails if a turn already exists, fabricates a fresh UUIDv7 sub-id, builds a default turn context and starts a `RegularTask` with `MailboxParentProvenance::Attribute` so the mailbox's parent/root turn ids are propagated onto the synthetic turn. It is invoked from three places: after an Interrupted abort, after an active turn is cleared in `on_task_finished`, and when the goal extension asks for continuation.
invariants: The wake must be idempotent against a live turn: the active-turn lock is taken and re-checked before a synthetic turn is created (core/src/tasks/mod.rs:474-480).

Mailbox provenance must be attributed only on the synthetic-wake path; otherwise a trigger-turn item whose root turn id disagrees marks the root turn ambiguous instead of overriding it (core/src/tasks/mod.rs:322-337).
Durable sleep is the only thing besides `trigger_turn` that may wake an idle thread — ordinary mailbox mail must not start a turn (core/src/tasks/mod.rs:467-472).
constants: Synthetic turn sub-id is a fresh `uuid::Uuid::new_v4()` (core/src/tasks/mod.rs:453)

loop.name: graceful-abort-with-history-marker
loop.what: `abort_all_tasks` / `abort_turn_if_active` take the active turn, cancel the task's cancellation token and then `select!` between the task's `done` Notify and a `GRACEFULL_INTERRUPTION_TIMEOUT_MS` sleep before force-aborting the JoinHandle — so a task gets a bounded window to unload cleanly. Pending approvals are cleared only after cancellation so an in-flight approval cannot surface as a model-visible rejection ahead of `TurnAborted`. For `Interrupted` and `BudgetLimited` abort reasons the session is marked interrupted, and an `InterruptedTurnHistoryMarker` item is recorded into conversation history and flushed *before* `TurnAborted` is emitted, because clients synchronously re-read the rollout on receipt. The marker's shape is version-dependent: `Disabled` when `agent_interrupt_message_enabled` is off, `Developer` role under `MultiAgentVersion::V2`, else a contextual-user fragment.
invariants: The interrupted-turn marker must be durably flushed before the TurnAborted event is emitted (core/src/tasks/mod.rs:932-937).
Pending approvals must be cleared after cancellation, never before, or an approval wait races the abort and appears to the model as a tool rejection (core/src/tasks/mod.rs:515-518, :560-562).
An abort of a task whose cancellation token is already cancelled is a no-op so the abort path cannot run twice (core/src/tasks/mod.rs:882-884).

loop.name: session-rollout-token-budget-ladder
loop.what: A session-tree-wide weighted token budget (`RolloutBudget`) accumulates `codex_rollout_budget_units` when the backend supplies them, otherwise `output_tokens * sampling_token_weight + non_cached_input * prefill_token_weight`, and reports exhaustion once the weighted total crosses `limit_tokens`. Before each sampling request `maybe_record_reminder` computes the remaining budget, counts how many configured `reminder_at_remaining_tokens` thresholds have been crossed, and records a `RolloutBudgetContext` fragment — but suppresses a repeat for the same (thread, window) unless a higher threshold index was crossed. Exhaustion surfaces as `CodexErr::SessionBudgetExceeded` from `record_rollout_budget_usage`. The whole budget is gated behind `Feature::RolloutBudget`, which is `Stage::UnderDevelopment` with `default_enabled: false` (features/src/lib.rs:1420-1425) — off unless explicitly enabled.
invariants: A reminder must be marked delivered only after the history insertion succeeds, so a cancelled insert is retried (core/src/rollout_budget.rs:99-110).
Backend-supplied budget units must be finite and non-negative; anything else is a fatal error rather than a silently ignored charge (core/src/rollout_budget.rs:50-58).
Reminders are per-thread so every thread in the tree observes a crossed threshold, not only the thread that happened to sample first (core/src/rollout_budget.rs:25-26, :82-86).
constants: Unconfigured budget is a no-op (`state.get()` is None -> Ok(false)) (core/src/rollout_budget.rs:120-126)

session.name: append-only-rollout-with-compacted-projection
session.what: Durable session state is an append-only JSONL rollout. `RolloutRecorder` owns a `tokio::mpsc` command channel to a background writer task (`AddItems`, `Persist`, `Flush`, `Shutdown` all carry oneshot acks), and the writer task's terminal IO failure is retained in a `Mutex<Option<Arc<IoError>>>` so a dead writer is observable rather than silently swallowing writes. Which items reach the file is decided by `is_persisted_rollout_item`: compaction, turn-context, world-state, security-score and session-meta markers are always persisted, `ItemCompleted` only in Paginated history mode, legacy message events only in Legacy mode, and transient events (deltas, begin/end tool events, warnings, guardian assessments, approvals) never. Compaction does not rewrite the file — it appends a `RolloutItem::Compacted` carrying `replacement_history`, and replay replaces the accumulated history with it, so the model-visible history is a projection over an unchanged log.
invariants: The rollout file is append-only; a compaction checkpoint must be appended, never used to rewrite prior lines (core/src/session/mod.rs:3391-3392 persists only `RolloutItem::Compacted`).
The world-state baseline must be persisted *after* the replacement history that established it (core/src/session/mod.rs:3393-3397).
Transient events must stay out of the rollout — `should_persist_event_msg` ends in an explicit `=> false` arm covering deltas, approvals, warnings and begin events (rollout/src/policy.rs:122-183).
constants: Filename shape `rollout-<timestamp>-<conversation_id>.jsonl`, with an optional `_<rollout_id>` suffix when `thread/revert` keeps the thread id but starts a new immutable rollout (rollout/src/recorder.rs:99-104)

session.name: rollout-reconstruction-on-resume
session.what: Resuming rebuilds the model-visible history by replaying a suffix of rollout items into a fresh `ContextManager`. A reverse scan stops at the newest `Compacted` item that carries a `replacement_history`, so the suffix starts from that checkpoint; the base replacement history is installed first and the suffix items are then replayed, with `InterAgentCommunication` items converted to model input and `ThreadRolledBack` events calling `history.drop_last_n_user_turns(n)`. Legacy compaction items with `replacement_history: None` take a second path: `collect_annotated_user_messages` plus `build_compacted_history` rebuild the summary, and the reference context item is deliberately cleared — the source notes this produces a temporary out-of-distribution prompt shape. `EventMsg`, `TurnContext`, `WorldState`, `SecurityRiskScore` and `SessionMeta` items contribute nothing to history reconstruction.
invariants: The reverse scan must stop before any compaction carrying a replacement history, so the loop's `Some(replacement_history)` branch is documented unreachable and exists only as defence (core/src/session/rollout_reconstruction.rs:345-348).
A legacy compaction without replacement history must clear the reference context item rather than guess one (core/src/session/rollout_reconstruction.rs:386-389).
`ThreadRolledBack` must be applied as a user-turn drop during replay, since it is a durable history mutation event (core/src/session/rollout_reconstruction.rs:369-371).
constants: fallback_window_number is derived by counting Compacted items, saturating to u64::MAX (core/src/session/rollout_reconstruction.rs:312-318)

session.name: six-database-sqlite-state-runtime
session.what: Durable non-transcript state lives in six separate SQLite files under the sqlite home (`state_5`, `logs_2`, `goals_1`, `memories_1`, `queue_1`, `thread_history_1`), each declared as a `RuntimeDbSpec` with its own sqlx `Migrator` compiled from a checked-in migrations directory (51 state migrations plus separate logs/goals/memories/queue/thread-history sets). Connections are opened with WAL journal mode and a 5 s busy timeout. `repair_legacy_recency_migration_version` hand-repairs the `_sqlx_migrations` row for version 39 only when the migration table exists, the checksum matches and the version is absent — an explicit compatibility shim for a previously shipped migration. A read-only single-connection pool exists for audit paths that must not migrate or repair.
invariants: Migrations must stay one directory per database; the migrators are compiled with `sqlx::migrate!` over distinct folders so a schema change cannot land in the wrong DB (state/src/migrations.rs:6-11).
The legacy repair must be a no-op unless the stored checksum equals the embedded one — it must never force-insert a migration row it did not verify (state/src/migrations.rs:56-118).
Known-but-newer migration versions are ignored, not rejected, so a downgraded binary still opens the DB (state/src/migrations.rs:16-21).
constants: STATE_DB_FILENAME = state_5.sqlite, LOGS_DB_FILENAME = logs_2.sqlite, GOALS_DB_FILENAME = goals_1.sqlite, MEMORIES_DB_FILENAME = memories_1.sqlite, QUEUE_DB_FILENAME = queue_1.sqlite, THREAD_HISTORY_DB_FILENAME = thread_history_1.sqlite (state/src/sqlite.rs:29-34)
50 state migrations + 2 queue + 4 thread_history + 2 goals + 1 memory + 2 logs (state/*_migrations/)

session.name: rollout-lineage-and-compression
session.what: Long-lived sessions are compacted on disk: `rollout/src/compression.rs` gz/zstd-compresses finished rollout files behind a run marker so only one compressor runs at a time, and lineage resolution walks `SessionMeta.history_base` pointers to assemble an ordered `RolloutLineage` of bounded segments, detecting cycles and coordinating with the writer lock while a referenced compressed segment is materialized. A `RolloutReferenceIndex` scans active and archived session directories keyed by immutable rollout id and computes inverse reference counts, with a deadline variant that returns no partial index.
invariants: Lineage resolution must fail closed on a repeated rollout id rather than loop (thread-store/src/local/rollout_lineage.rs:92-94).
A reference-index scan past its deadline returns None, never a truncated index (rollout/src/rollout_reference_index.rs:48-64).
A rollout's own history_base equal to its own id is not a reference (rollout/src/rollout_reference_index.rs:146-156).
constants: compression::WORKER_MAX_RUNTIME = 5 h, RUN_MARKER_STALE_AFTER = 6 h, COMPRESSION_LEVEL = 3, COMPRESSED_SUFFIX = .zst, RUN_MARKER_FILE_NAME = rollout-compression.lock (rollout/src/compression.rs:24-31, :183-186)

session.name: durable-queued-user-submissions
session.what: `codex queue --thread <id> --message <text>` does not write to the in-memory input queue; it persists a row into the `queued_items` SQLite table (id PK, thread_id, payload_json, queue_order with UNIQUE(thread_id, queue_order)) behind the storage-neutral `QueueStore` trait. `QueuedItemService` drains items one at a time into an idle thread and deletes each only after the submission reports `StartIfIdleSubmission::Started`, so a rejected start leaves the item queued. A background `watch_external_messages` task ticks every 10 s, checks SQLite's inexpensive data version, then uses the `queued_thread_revisions` table (maintained by AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE triggers) to find only changed threads and spawns an independent per-thread dispatch task, so one blocked thread cannot starve the others. Item count is capped per thread.
invariants: FIFO per thread is load-bearing: dispatch always reads page size 1 from offset 0 and deletes only on a Started submission (ext/queue/src/service.rs:226-236).
The per-thread cap MAX_QUEUE_ITEMS = 100 must be enforced at enqueue (state/src/lib.rs:94).
Revision bookkeeping must be trigger-maintained so external writers are seen without polling the items table (state/queue_migrations/0002_queued_thread_revisions.sql:9-34).
constants: watch_external_messages interval = 10 s; per-thread dispatch retry sleep = 10 s (ext/queue/src/service.rs:88-95, :238)
Only user-message input may be enqueued; QueueServiceError::InvalidInput otherwise (ext/queue/src/service.rs:56-61)

session.name: global-message-history-jsonl
session.what: A separate global append-only `~/.codex/history.jsonl` records one JSON object per line (`{session_id, ts, text}`) for every user message, independent of the per-session rollout. The module documents the write contract explicitly: prepare the full line including the trailing newline and write it in a single `write(2)` with the descriptor opened `O_APPEND`, relying on the POSIX guarantee that writes up to `PIPE_BUF` are atomic, so concurrent processes cannot interleave partial records. Reads use buffered line iteration.
invariants: A record must be written as one full line in one `write(2)` with O_APPEND — splitting the record across writes breaks the atomicity the concurrency story depends on (message-history/src/lib.rs:11-15).
The record schema is fixed at {session_id, ts, text}; appending a field requires a reader-side story because the file is never rewritten (message-history/src/lib.rs:6-9).

context.name: pre-sampling-compaction-with-provider-routing
context.what: Compaction runs *before* the sampling request, in `run_pre_sampling_compact` at the head of `run_turn`, and again mid-turn when the token status says the window is exhausted. `/compact` dispatches to `CompactTask`, which selects one of three implementations by provider capability: `compact_token_budget::run_manual_compact_task` when `Feature::TokenBudget` is on; `compact_remote::run_remote_compact_task` or `compact_remote_v2::run_remote_compact_task` when the provider advertises `RemoteCompactionSupport::V1`/`V2` (server-side compaction, with a `codex-api` endpoint at endpoint/compact.rs:39); and otherwise the local `compact::run_compact_task`, which sends the templated `SUMMARIZATION_PROMPT` as an extra `UserInput` round, takes the last assistant message as the summary, prepends `SUMMARY_PREFIX` and rebuilds history from the recent user messages up to a token cap. Any non-abort, non-tool-collision failure of the pre-sampling compaction is absorbed: the error is logged and the function returns `Ok(None)` rather than failing the turn.
invariants: Compaction must never write a new history in place — it publishes a checkpoint plus a replacement history and keeps the original events (core/src/session/mod.rs:3367-3392).
Provider capability routing must be explicit: remote compaction is only attempted when the provider advertises support, never optimistically (core/src/tasks/compact.rs:19-85).
A compaction failure must not surface as a turn failure when the cause is not an abort or a tool collision (core/src/session/turn.rs:182-190).
constants: Auto-compaction emits a warning after compaction that long threads reduce accuracy (core/src/compact.rs:389-392)

context.name: context-window-token-status-and-compact-scope
context.what: `context_window_token_status` produces the single token verdict the turn loop consults. It counts usage against one of two scopes: `AutoCompactTokenLimitScope::Total` charges the model's whole `auto_compact_token_limit`, while `BodyAfterPrefix` subtracts a persisted prefill baseline so only tokens added after the window prefix count, with a per-config `model_auto_compact_token_limit` overriding the model's own. Independently it computes the model's *full* context window as a hard cap, takes the minimum of the two remaining-token figures as the reported headroom, and adds the configured `auto_compact_fallback_buffer_tokens` to the compact limit before declaring `token_limit_reached`. The turn loop uses `token_limit_reached` (or an explicit new-context-window request) to decide to roll over into auto-compaction.
invariants: The full context window is a hard cap independent of the auto-compaction scope — reaching it forces compaction even when the compact scope still has headroom (core/src/session/context_window.rs:53-79).
The fallback buffer is only reserved when a fallback prompt actually exists to consume it (core/src/session/context_window.rs:65-72).
Compaction starts a new history window, so its world-state baseline must be a full snapshot rather than a diff (core/src/session/mod.rs:3379-3388).
constants: Auto-compact derivation from the catalogue = context_window * 9 / 10 (protocol/src/openai_models.rs, cited via the model domain)
Window ids are UUIDv7 with first/previous/current chained across compaction (core/src/state/auto_compact_window.rs:1-20, :77-80)

context.name: token-budget-reminder-and-compact-fallback
context.what: A model-owned or user-owned token budget injects two different contextual fragments. When remaining tokens against the *unbuffered* base window are at or below `reminder_threshold_tokens`, a one-shot `TokenBudgetReminder` fragment carrying the remaining count is claimed through session state and recorded into history. When no auto-compact fallback is allowed and remaining tokens have hit exactly zero, a one-shot `AutoCompactFallbackPrompt` fragment is injected instead. Model-provided defaults are applied only when the feature is on and the user has set nothing: `apply_model_defaults` copies `reminder_threshold_tokens`, `reminder_message_template`, `guidance_message`, `auto_compact_fallback_prompt` and `auto_compact_fallback_buffer_tokens` out of the model catalogue and validates them, logging and discarding an invalid set rather than failing. `Feature::TokenBudget` is `Stage::UnderDevelopment` with `default_enabled: false` (features/src/lib.rs:1414-1419), so this is off unless enabled.
invariants: Each reminder must fire at most once per claimed state — delivery is claimed through `Session::state` before the fragment is recorded (core/src/session/token_budget.rs:79-92, :101-107).
Invalid model-owned defaults must be discarded with a warning, never applied partially (core/src/session/token_budget.rs:46-53).
Explicit user settings win over model defaults; the model defaults are only a fallback (core/src/session/token_budget.rs:23-26).
constants: TokenBudgetConfig fields: reminder_threshold_tokens, reminder_message_template, guidance_message, auto_compact_fallback_prompt, auto_compact_fallback_buffer_tokens (core/src/session/token_budget.rs:36-44)

context.name: world-state-section-diffing
context.what: Instead of re-injecting a monolithic context blurb every turn, model-visible environment state is a keyed set of typed `WorldStateSection`s (agents_md, apps, collaboration mode, compact permissions, context-window guidance, environments, model, multi-agent mode, multi-agent usage hint, permissions, personality, plugins, realtime, tools). Each section snapshots itself to a compact JSON value; the live `WorldState` renders, for each changed section, a `ContextualUserFragment` diff against the previous snapshot, and the snapshot set is diffed into an RFC 7386 merge patch that is persisted as a `WorldStateItem` so a resumed session can reconstruct the previous state without replaying every fragment. A `WorldStateHash` is a SHA-1 over `role` plus rendered text with a versioned domain separator, used to recognize a fragment already present in retained history.
invariants: A section `ID` is persisted in rollouts and must remain stable across releases (core/src/context/world_state/mod.rs:202-212).

A section snapshot must never serialize to null, because merge-patch null means deletion — the erased wrapper refuses a null snapshot with an error log (core/src/context/world_state/mod.rs:206-209, :84-90).
Removals must be emitted before insertions in the generated patch so the patch output order is stable (core/src/context/world_state/mod.rs:299-305).
constants: Patch format is RFC 7386 merge patch (`merge_patch_from` / `apply_merge_patch`) (core/src/context/world_state/mod.rs:297-330)
Fragment hash domain separator `codex-world-state-fragment-v1\0`, CRLF normalized to LF, length-prefixed components (core/src/context/world_state/mod.rs:252-266)

context.name: contextual-fragment-injection-primitive
context.what: Every piece of injected context (environment, permissions, AGENTS.md, hooks, skills, inter-agent messages, token-budget reminders, aborted-turn markers, image notices, model-switch notes) is a `ContextualUserFragment` implementation rather than a bespoke message: the trait owns the response `role()`, a body, and a pair of start/end markers, and `render()` concatenates markers and body while `matches_text` recognizes a previously injected fragment of that type in existing history. Markers are the mechanism that lets world-state diffing and compaction tell an injected fragment apart from genuine user text. Over 35 fragment types are registered in one module.
invariants: Role ownership belongs to the fragment, not the caller — a fragment decides whether it is a developer or user message (context-fragments/src/fragment.rs:14-15).
Unmarked fragments must leave both markers empty, in which case `matches_text` must never match arbitrary text (context-fragments/src/fragment.rs:8-13).
Marker text is part of the persisted transcript, so changing a marker is a history-compatibility change.
constants: `requires_separate_message()` defaults to false, letting a fragment share a message with others unless it opts out (context-fragments/src/fragment.rs:17-20)

tools.name: tool-registry-with-exposure-ladder
tools.what: All model-callable tools live in one `ToolRegistry` keyed by `ToolName` (optionally namespaced) mapping to a `RegisteredTool { runtime, exposure }`. Exposure is derived from three independent booleans (direct-model, deferred, code-mode) into exactly one of `Hidden`, `CodeModeOnly`, `DirectModelOnly`, `Direct`, `DeferredModelOnly`, `Deferred`; direct and deferred are mutually exclusive and their combination is an `unreachable!`. Built-in names are collision-fatal (`error_or_panic!` on a duplicate registration, and the literal name shell_command is reserved against external registration), whereas externally supplied tools (MCP/plugins) are admitted only into vacant slots, recording the first collision and warning instead of panicking. Deferred namespaces can advertise a namespace description even when the tools themselves are not in the request.
invariants: A duplicate trusted registration is a bug, not a shadowing opportunity — `register_trusted_with_exposure` calls `error_or_panic!` (core/src/tools/registry.rs:319-328).
The `shell_command` name is reserved: external tools with that name are skipped and recorded as a collision (core/src/tools/registry.rs:352-359).
Direct and deferred exposure must never both be true — the mapping is exhaustive with an `unreachable!` arm (core/src/tools/spec_plan.rs:237-246).
constants: Exposure ladder: Hidden / CodeModeOnly / DirectModelOnly / Direct / DeferredModelOnly / Deferred (core/src/tools/spec_plan.rs:240-246)
Feature::ToolSearch and Feature::ToolSearchAlwaysDeferMcpTools are both Stage::Removed (features/src/lib.rs:1169-1177); Feature::ToolSuggest is Stable default true (features/src/lib.rs:1199-1201)

tools.name: parallel-tool-dispatch-with-serialization-gate
tools.what: `ToolCallRuntime::handle_tool_call_with_source` spawns each tool call onto its own Tokio task and then takes an admission gate: tools that advertise `supports_parallel_tool_calls` take a shared read lock on an `RwLock<()>`, everything else takes the exclusive write lock, so parallel-safe calls overlap while mutating tools serialize against each other and against the parallel group. A `ToolCallTimingGuard` records the instant the gate is acquired so dispatch wait time and handler time are separable in telemetry. Cancellation is a `tokio::select!` between the dispatch handle and the turn cancellation token; on abort the runtime consults `waits_for_runtime_cancellation` — runtimes that need teardown are awaited instead of aborted, so a process-backed tool can finish cleanup before the model sees the aborted-output notice.
invariants: Timing attribution must stay split: `execution_started_at` is set only after the gate is acquired, so dispatch latency is never attributed to the handler (core/src/tools/parallel.rs:158-162, :324-332).
A runtime that declares `waits_for_runtime_cancellation` must not be force-aborted on cancellation; it is awaited so teardown completes (core/src/tools/parallel.rs:188-198).

Only one of the two dispatch paths may claim the terminal outcome (`terminal_outcome_reached` compare-exchange), so an abort and a completion cannot both produce a final result (core/src/tools/parallel.rs:183-191).
constants: A tool failure becomes a model-visible `FunctionCallOutput` with `success: Some(false)` for payloads other than ToolSearch/Custom, which get their own output shapes (core/src/tools/parallel.rs:230-255)
Aborted-output text is `aborted by user after {secs:.1}s`, or `Wall time: {secs:.1} seconds\naborted by user` for shell_command/unified_exec (core/src/tools/parallel.rs:268-279)

tools.name: approval-sandbox-retry-orchestrator
tools.what: `ToolOrchestrator::run` implements one fixed sequence for every tool runtime: (1) compute the `ExecApprovalRequirement` — a tool may supply its own, otherwise `default_exec_approval_requirement` derives one from the approval policy and the filesystem sandbox policy — then either skip, hard-reject `Forbidden`, or request approval; a `strict_auto_review` turn forces an approval request even on `Skip` so the guardian sees every action. (2) Select the sandbox for the first attempt, honouring `BypassSandboxFirstAttempt`. (3) On a `SandboxErr::Denied`, decide whether a retry is even legal: no escalation if the tool refuses it, if the policy forbids unsandboxed execution, or if no network approval context exists; otherwise request a second approval (unless the tool may bypass it) and re-run with the escalated sandbox. Sandbox outcomes (`denied`, `timed_out`, `signal`, `escalated`) are emitted to telemetry with both attempt durations.
invariants: A sandboxed attempt's approval must not authorise the unsandboxed retry: under strict auto-review the retry always requires a fresh review (core/src/tools/orchestrator.rs:391-395).
Under `Never` or `OnRequest` a denial must not silently retry without a sandbox — the denial output is preserved and returned (core/src/tools/orchestrator.rs:344-370).
There are exactly two attempts; there is no third escalation tier (core/src/tools/orchestrator.rs:282-289 and :465-469).
constants: Escalation-denial reason string is the stable literal "command failed; retry without sandbox?" (core/src/tools/orchestrator.rs:527-531)
Network escalation reason is `Network access to "{host}" is blocked by policy.` (core/src/tools/orchestrator.rs:381-389)
Sandbox outcome tags recorded: denied / timed_out / signal / escalated (core/src/tools/orchestrator.rs:515-525)

tools.name: unified-pty-exec-process-manager
tools.what: The default shell tool is a single PTY-backed session manager rather than one-shot command execution: `unified_exec` spawns a process, yields output for a bounded window, and keeps the process alive as a background terminal that later calls can write to and read from. Yield time is clamped into a range with a raised floor on Windows for the first exec, an empty-output yield gets a longer floor, background terminals get a long default maximum timeout, and the number of concurrently tracked processes is capped. Per-process output is not truncated by dropping the tail: a symmetric `HeadTailBuffer` keeps 50% of the byte budget as a stable prefix and 50% as a suffix and inserts an explicit omission marker with the dropped byte count.
invariants: Output truncation must preserve both ends of the stream and report how much was dropped; it must never silently keep only the head (core/src/unified_exec/head_tail_buffer.rs:5-10, :74-95).
The tracked-process count is capped at MAX_UNIFIED_EXEC_PROCESSES; a spawn past the cap must be refused rather than leaking a process (core/src/unified_exec/mod.rs:75).
A late network denial arriving just after a process start is granted a grace period rather than killing the process immediately (core/src/unified_exec/process_manager.rs:95-98).

tools.name: streaming-patch-application
tools.what: File modification is a dedicated `apply_patch` tool with its own Lark grammar (core/src/tools/handlers/apply_patch.lark) parsed into `ApplyPatchAction`, which is then handed to `codex_apply_patch` for execution. Because the patch text is generated token-by-token, partial input is consumed by a `ToolArgumentDiffConsumer` that emits patch-progress protocol events while arguments stream, and the tool participates in the turn diff tracker so a turn's net file changes can be reported as a `TurnDiffEvent`. Two behaviours are feature-gated: streaming progress events and line-ending preservation are both `Stage::UnderDevelopment` with `default_enabled: false` (features/src/lib.rs:1021-1031). A separate `assess_patch_safety` gate decides whether the patch may be auto-approved.
invariants: A patch that appears confined to writable roots must still be executed inside a sandbox, because a path may be a hard link to a file outside those roots (core/src/safety.rs:57-59).

Auto-approval requires that a platform sandbox can actually be enforced; when none is available the patch is escalated to the user, or rejected if the policy refuses sandbox approvals (core/src/safety.rs:69-89).
An empty patch is rejected outright rather than treated as a no-op success (core/src/safety.rs:34-38).
constants: Rejection reasons: "writing outside of the project; rejected by user approval settings" and "writing is blocked by read-only sandbox; rejected by user approval settings" (core/src/safety.rs:14-17)

Feature::ApplyPatchStreamingEvents and Feature::ApplyPatchPreserveLineEndings both UnderDevelopment/OFF (features/src/lib.rs:1021-1031); Feature::ApplyPatchFreeform is Stage::Removed (features/src/lib.rs:1015-1017)

tools.name: exec-policy-rules-and-durable-amendment
tools.what: An executable-policy layer classifies shell commands by prefix rule into `Decision::{Allow, Prompt, Forbidden}` and network rules (host + protocol) into allow/prompt/deny, and can *amend* the policy file at runtime: `blocking_append_allow_prefix_rule` serializes a `prefix_rule(pattern=[...], decision="allow")` line, and `blocking_append_network_rule` serializes a host/protocol/decision/justification rule, both taking an advisory file lock and appending to the policy file. Because both use advisory locking and blocking IO, callers must run them under `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`. Approval responses can carry the amendment (`ReviewDecision::ApprovedExecpolicyAmendment`, `NetworkPolicyAmendment`) so a single user decision both permits this call and persists a rule for future ones.
invariants: Policy amendments must hold the advisory file lock and must be executed on a blocking thread, never directly on an async executor thread (execpolicy/src/amend.rs:63-68).
An empty prefix is rejected before any file is touched (execpolicy/src/amend.rs:69-71).
A network rule justification, if supplied, must be non-empty (execpolicy/src/amend.rs:94-100).
constants: Decision wire strings allow / prompt / deny (execpolicy/src/amend.rs:106-111)
Feature::RequestRule is Stage::Removed (features/src/lib.rs:1063-1065), so the model-facing rule-request path is dead; the amendment path itself is live

tools.name: filesystem-and-search-tool-runtimes
tools.what: Read-oriented local capability is a set of runtimes over two crates rather than ad-hoc file IO: `file-system` provides a sandbox-aware filesystem abstraction whose call sites can be run with the narrower `SandboxManager::for_file_system_helpers()` profile, and `file-search` provides a streaming nucleo-backed fuzzy path search with a walker thread and matcher thread joined by a channel, gitignore scoping tied to real git repositories, a bounded cancellation check interval and NonZero limit/thread settings. `utils/output-truncation` supplies the shared token/line truncation policy (`TruncationPolicy`, `truncate_text`, `formatted_truncate_text`) that every tool applies to model-facing output. There is no LSP client and no `codex-rs/lsp` crate in this checkout — the LSP entries in the seed list come from other sources.
invariants: Fuzzy search walkers must poll for cancellation at a bounded interval rather than running to completion (file-search/src/lib.rs:455-492).

`.gitignore` handling must only be active inside a git context; disabling it must turn off git ignore, git global, git exclude, .ignore and parent scanning together (file-search/src/lib.rs:111-118, :431-447).
Filesystem helper operations must run under the narrower file-system-helper sandbox profile, not the full agent profile (sandboxing/src/manager.rs:285-291).
constants: FileSearchOptions defaults: limit = 20, threads = 2, respect_gitignore = true, compute_indices = false (file-search/src/lib.rs:121-132)
Truncation policy multiplier used for historical function outputs is 1.2x (core/src/tools/context.rs:140-145)

tools.name: pre-main-process-hardening
tools.what: The binary hardens itself before `main()` via `#[ctor::ctor]`, on the theory that a compromised environment should not be able to attach to the agent process. On Linux/Android it clears `PR_SET_DUMPABLE`, sets the core-file-size rlimit to zero and strips `LD_*` environment variables; macOS does the equivalent with `PTRACE_DENY_ATTACH` and `DYLD_*`; FreeBSD/OpenBSD use the BSD variant; Windows has its own path. Each hardening step has a dedicated non-zero exit code, so a process that could not harden itself exits rather than continuing unhardened.
invariants: Hardening failures must terminate the process with the step's specific exit code — the process must not continue unhardened (process-hardening/src/lib.rs:46-53)
Environment scrubbing must happen pre-main so no later code observes a poisoned variable (process-hardening/src/lib.rs:7-11)

subagent.name: spawn-agent-tool-with-context-fork
subagent.what: Delegation is a namespaced tool (`multi_agent_v1` namespace, `spawn_agent`) that resolves the child's session source with `next_thread_spawn_depth`, refuses to spawn past `config.agent_max_depth` with the model-facing message 'Agent depth limit reached. Solve the task yourself.', builds a child config by cloning base instructions, optionally applying a role and model/reasoning-effort/service-tier overrides, and then calls `agent_control.spawn_agent_with_metadata`. `fork_context: true` requests a `SpawnAgentForkMode::FullHistory` fork and is incompatible with a role override (rejected explicitly); a full fork also inherits the parent model, so a model override is not accepted alongside it. The tool emits a `CollabAgentToolCall` turn item in InProgress and then Completed state with the resolved nickname, role and model.
invariants: Depth must be enforced before spawn, using `exceeds_thread_spawn_depth_limit(child_depth, max_depth)` (core/src/tools/handlers/multi_agents/spawn.rs:65-71).
A full-history fork may not also override the agent type (core/src/tools/handlers/multi_agents/spawn.rs:94-96).
A failed spawn must still produce a Completed turn item with `AgentStatus::NotFound`, so the parent's transcript records the attempt (core/src/tools/handlers/multi_agents/spawn.rs:139-146, :192-208).

subagent.name: v1-and-v2-agent-control-toolsets
subagent.what: Two parallel control surfaces exist. V1 (namespace `multi_agent_v1`) offers `spawn_agent`, `send_input`, `wait_agent`, `close_agent` and `resume_agent`; V2 exposes the same operations as flat tools alongside team-oriented additions — `followup_task` (give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn), `send_message` (deliver without triggering a turn), `interrupt_agent` and `list_agents`. `wait_agent` is bounded by a configurable timeout: V1 uses fixed default/min/max values, while V2 reads per-turn `min_wait_timeout_ms` / `max_wait_timeout_ms` / `default_wait_timeout_ms` from `MultiAgentV2Config` and clamps the requested timeout into that range. `resume_agent` re-checks the spawn depth limit, so resuming cannot be used to exceed the depth cap. `Feature::MultiAgentV2` is `Stage::Stable` with `default_enabled: false` (features/src/lib.rs:1121-1123), so the V2 surface is off unless enabled; `Feature::MultiAgentMode` and `Feature::SpawnCsv` are `Stage::Removed` (features/src/lib.rs:1127-1135).
invariants: A wait timeout must be clamped into the configured range and must be greater than zero (core/src/tools/handlers/multi_agents/wait.rs:89-93, multi_agents_v2/wait.rs:49-53).
Resume must re-apply the depth limit; it is not a way to bypass spawn depth (core/src/tools/handlers/multi_agents/resume_agent.rs:53-54).

Interrupt and close must resolve the target through `agent_control` rather than acting on a raw thread id supplied by the model (core/src/tools/handlers/multi_agents_v2/interrupt_agent.rs:38, multi_agents/close_agent.rs:72-75).
constants: V2 defaults: min 10_000 ms, max 3_600_000 ms, default 30_000 ms (core/src/config/mod.rs:221-223)
Features MultiAgentMode and SpawnCsv (key 'enable_fanout') are Stage::Removed (features/src/lib.rs:1127-1135)

subagent.name: inter-agent-mailbox-with-turn-trigger
subagent.what: Agents communicate through a mailbox that is a distinct tier of `TurnInput` (`InterAgentCommunication`), not a side channel. `InputQueue` holds a `VecDeque<PendingMailboxCommunication>` with parent and root turn ids and a diagnostics gauge, and a `watch` channel whose value is `InputQueueActivity::{Mailbox, Steer}` gives subscribers a cheap liveness signal. Mail is delivered in two modes: mail marked `trigger_turn` (or any mail while a durable sleep is outstanding) can start a synthetic turn on an idle thread, while ordinary mail is only drained into an active turn. `accept_mailbox_delivery_for_current_turn` is called exactly when the model still needs follow-up, so a message is not injected into a turn that is ending.
invariants: Mailbox mail must not be folded into the user-input tier — it is its own `TurnInput` variant and carries its own provenance metadata (core/src/session/input_queue.rs:19-30, :82-87).
A root turn id on incoming mail that disagrees with the turn's recorded root marks the root turn ambiguous rather than overwriting it (core/src/session/turn_input.rs:550-557).
Mail delivery to the current turn may only be accepted when the model requested follow-up (core/src/session/turn.rs:402-409).

subagent.name: thread-spawn-topology-graph-store
subagent.what: Parent/child topology is persisted, not just held in memory: a storage-neutral `AgentGraphStore` trait records directional thread-spawn edges with an open/closed status, with a `LocalAgentGraphStore` implementation delegating to the SQLite state runtime. The trait exposes direct-children listing and breadth-first descendant listing in which the status filter is applied to every traversed edge, so descendants behind a closed edge are excluded even when their own edge is open. List methods are required to return stable ordering so persisted graph state can be merged with live in-memory state deterministically. The in-memory counterpart is `AgentRegistry`, which additionally enforces the per-session thread count and allocates human-readable agent paths and nicknames.
invariants: A child thread has at most one persisted parent; re-inserting the same child updates parent and status instead of creating a parallel edge (agent-graph-store/src/store.rs:18-27).
Descendant traversal must apply the status filter to traversed edges, not only to returned nodes (agent-graph-store/src/store.rs:49-59).
List ordering must be stable so persisted and live views can be merged deterministically (agent-graph-store/src/store.rs:13-16).
constants: AgentRegistry total-count reservation errors with `CodexErrorDetails::AgentLimitReached { max_threads }` (core/src/agent/registry.rs:96-115)

subagent.name: agent-path-identity-and-nicknames
subagent.what: Each agent has a stable logical path, an `AgentPath` newtype validated as an absolute slash path with `/root` and `/morpheus` as named roots, supporting `join` and `resolve` (including relative references resolved against the current agent's own path). `AgentControl::resolve_agent_reference` resolves a reference from a model-supplied string to a live thread id through the registry and returns `UnsupportedOperation("live agent path `{}` not found")` on a miss, so a stale path cannot silently address a different agent. Human-readable nicknames are allocated from a built-in name list and disambiguated by an ordinal suffix ('the 2nd', 'the 3rd') on reuse, tracked in `used_agent_nicknames` with a reset counter. Separately, `agent-identity` implements the cryptographic service identity for ChatGPT-hosted agent tasks: it generates Ed25519/Curve25519 key material, signs a task-registration payload, decodes a JWKS-verified identity JWT with audience `codex-app-server`, and decrypts the task-id response.
invariants: An agent path must be absolute and validated at construction; `from_string` rejects a non-absolute path (protocol/src/agent_path.rs:30-33).
Path resolution must go through the live registry and fail rather than fall back to another agent (core/src/agent/control.rs:384-403).
An agent-identity JWT must be decoded with the expected audience and against fetched JWKS, not trusted unverified (agent-identity/src/lib.rs:266-305).

subagent.name: goal-durable-continuation
subagent.what: A goal is durable state, not a prompt convention: one row per thread in the SQLite `thread_goals` table with a CHECK-constrained status (active/paused/blocked/usage_limited/budget_limited/complete), a token budget and accrued usage. When a thread goes idle, `GoalExtension::on_thread_idle` calls `GoalRuntimeHandle::continue_if_idle`, which re-reads the row and — only if the status is exactly `Active` — injects a continuation steering item and calls `start_turn_if_idle` to reopen the thread; for any other status it clears the active-goal accounting and returns without starting a turn. Writes are serialized by a per-thread `Semaphore(1)` so an external set/clear cannot interleave with the read-then-write, and usage accrual is guarded by an expected goal id. `Feature::Goals` is `Stage::Stable` with `default_enabled: true`.
invariants: Continuation may only start when the persisted status is exactly `Active`; every other status clears accounting and does not start a turn (ext/goal/src/runtime.rs:399-405).
Every goal write must be serialized by the per-thread goal_state_lock together with the progress-accounting lock (ext/goal/src/runtime.rs:367-369).
Usage may only be charged against the goal_id the caller expected, so a stale writer cannot mutate a replaced goal.
constants: No enforced auto-continuation round counter exists in code; the nearest construct is prompt-level policy text in ext/goal/templates/goals/continuation.md

safety.name: permission-profile-model-with-requirement-allowed-catalog
safety.what: Permissions are a resolved profile, not a mode enum. `PermissionProfile` is `Managed { file_system, network, enforcement }`, `Disabled`, or `External { .. }`; the filesystem half is a `FileSystemSandboxPolicy` of explicit read/write entries over absolute paths and *special* paths, with per-entry mode, a per-entry missing-path behaviour, a skip-missing flag and a `ReadDenyMatcher` supporting deny-read globs. Three built-in profiles are always offered (read-only, workspace-write, danger-full-access); user-defined profiles from `permissions` config are appended, and each entry's `allowed` flag is computed from three requirement sources — the allowed-profile-names list, the sandbox-mode requirement, and a deny-read compatibility check that refuses a danger-full-access or external profile when requirements declare deny-read paths. Approval granularity is a five-flag `GranularApprovalConfig` (sandbox_approval, rules, skill_approval, request_permissions, mcp_elicitations), where a false flag means the request is auto-rejected rather than shown to the user.
invariants: A profile may only be offered if all three requirement checks agree; the catalog computes `allowed` rather than trusting the config (core/src/config/permission_profile_catalog.rs:98-122).

A deny-read requirement must not be satisfied by a danger-full-access or external profile — that combination is a hard constraint error listing the allowed values (core/src/config/permission_profile_catalog.rs:124-139).
Under `Granular`, a false flag must reject the request instead of prompting, so the flags are fail-closed by construction (protocol/src/protocol.rs:928-938).

`AskForApproval` has removed variants that must not be reintroduced: the active set is `UnlessTrusted | OnRequest | Granular | Never`, with `on-failure` accepted only as a serde alias for OnRequest (protocol/src/protocol.rs:914-939).
constants: Built-in profile ids: BUILT_IN_READ_ONLY_PROFILE, BUILT_IN_WORKSPACE_PROFILE, BUILT_IN_DANGER_FULL_ACCESS_PROFILE (core/src/config/permission_profile_catalog.rs:13-15, :53-70)

`ReviewDecision` variants: Approved, ApprovedExecpolicyAmendment, ApprovedForSession, ApprovedMcpPolicyAmendment, NetworkPolicyAmendment, Denied{rejection}, TimedOut, Abort; `Default` is `Denied { rejection: "denied" }` (protocol/src/protocol.rs:3868-3912)

safety.name: session-scoped-approval-cache
safety.what: Approvals are cached per session keyed by a serialized *set* of keys, because one tool call can touch several resources (apply_patch may modify multiple files). `with_cached_approval` short-circuits to `ApprovedForSession` only when every key in the request is already approved; otherwise it fetches a fresh decision, emits a `codex.approval.requested` counter tagged with tool and outcome, and stores `ApprovedForSession` for each key individually, so a later request touching any subset also skips prompting. An empty key set deliberately bypasses the cache entirely rather than being treated as pre-approved.
invariants: All keys must be approved for the cache to hit — a partial match must still prompt (core/src/tools/sandboxing.rs:87-95).
An empty key vector must not hit the cache; it fetches unconditionally as a defensive measure (core/src/tools/sandboxing.rs:82-85).
A session decision is stored per key, not per request, so it generalizes to subsets (core/src/tools/sandboxing.rs:108-113).
constants: Cache key is the JSON serialization of the caller's key value (core/src/tools/sandboxing.rs:46-61)

safety.name: platform-sandbox-selection-and-transform
safety.what: `SandboxManager` owns selection and command transformation. `should_sandbox` returns false for `SandboxablePreference::Forbid`, true for `Require`, and for `Auto` defers to the filesystem/network policy plus whether managed network requirements are active; `select_initial` then asks `get_platform_sandbox` for the host's concrete backend, which is seatbelt on macOS, seccomp/landlock on Linux, and the Windows restricted-token backend only when the Windows sandbox level is not `Disabled`. `transform` rewrites argv per backend: seatbelt prepends `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` with a generated profile; Linux prepends the `codex-linux-sandbox` helper with an arg0 override and a serialized permission profile, and refuses to run on WSL1 when bubblewrap is required; Windows returns the argv unchanged here and is wrapped later by `transform_for_direct_spawn`, which additionally refuses managed networking unless the elevated backend is selected.
invariants: Managed networking on Windows requires the elevated backend — a restricted-token transform returns a preparation error instead of proceeding (sandboxing/src/manager.rs:440-446).
A missing Linux sandbox executable is an error, not a silent unsandboxed fallback (sandboxing/src/manager.rs:408-410).
The effective permission profile must be carried through the transform result so downstream code sees what was actually enforced, not what was requested (sandboxing/src/manager.rs:461-481).

safety.name: seatbelt-and-bubblewrap-backends
safety.what: macOS confinement generates a Seatbelt profile per invocation from four bundled `.sbpl` sources (base policy, network policy, restricted read-only platform defaults, process-applications read policy) plus dynamically built allow/deny entries: access roots with per-root read/write kinds, protected-metadata-name regexes for writable roots, unreadable glob policies converted to Seatbelt regexes, and a dynamic network policy that allows only the loopback ports of the managed proxy and the Unix socket paths that the proxy needs. Linux confinement invokes a `codex-linux-sandbox` helper that applies in-process `no_new_privs` plus seccomp and uses bubblewrap for filesystem isolation, with a bundled bubblewrap that is digest-verified. On WSL1 the transform is refused rather than degraded.
invariants: The bundled bubblewrap must be digest-verified; a verification failure exits with a dedicated code instead of running an unverified helper (linux-sandbox/src/lib.rs:27-29).
Unreadable-glob expansion is capped so a glob cannot be turned into an unbounded profile (linux-sandbox/src/bwrap.rs:56).
Seatbelt network policy must be derived from the actual proxy configuration, not a static allow-all (sandboxing/src/seatbelt.rs:288-363).
constants: FORWARDED_SIGNALS list plus BWRAP_CHILD_PID / PENDING_FORWARDED_SIGNAL atomics (linux-sandbox/src/linux_run_main.rs:41-44)
Feature::UseLinuxSandboxBwrap is Stage::Removed; Feature::UseLegacyLandlock is Stage::Deprecated default false (features/src/lib.rs:1051-1059)

safety.name: windows-sandbox-three-levels-with-wfp
safety.what: Windows has two concrete backends behind a three-valued `WindowsSandboxLevel { Disabled, RestrictedToken, Elevated }`. The restricted-token backend creates a WRITE_RESTRICTED token for spawn; the code is explicit about what it cannot do — its capability SIDs do not participate in read access checks, so it refuses (with 'refusing to run unsandboxed') to handle split read restrictions, deny-read paths, differing writable-root sets, or writable descendants reopened under a read-only carveout, and it can only layer deny-write carveouts on top of the legacy writable allow set. The elevated backend uses a separate offline local user identity plus ACLs and WFP network filters, supports explicit read/write root overrides and deny-read paths, and is required for managed networking and for a proxy restricting SID. The startup dispatch is one match on the sandbox level.
invariants: The restricted-token backend must refuse rather than run unsandboxed whenever it cannot enforce the requested policy; the failure strings are literal and load-bearing (sandboxing/src/windows.rs:96-102, :113-129, :147-169).
Managed networking must not be attempted on the restricted-token backend — the spawner bails, and the transform errors earlier (windows-sandbox-rs/src/unified_exec/mod.rs:74-79).
Skip-missing path entries must be removed before computing overrides, so a not-yet-existing path is not turned into a deny-write sentinel (sandboxing/src/windows.rs:104-107).
constants: WFP filters defined statically: ICMP connect/assign v4+v6, DNS 53 v4+v6, DNS-over-TLS 853 v4+v6, SMB 445 v4+v6, SMB 139 v4+v6, all scoped by the sandbox user (windows-sandbox-rs/src/wfp/filter_specs.rs:25-124)
NAME_RESOLUTION_CACHE filters are deliberately omitted because their static shapes failed validation with FWP_E_OUT_OF_BOUNDS (windows-sandbox-rs/src/wfp/filter_specs.rs:66-67)
Feature::WindowsSandbox (key experimental_windows_sandbox) and Feature::WindowsSandboxElevated (elevated_windows_sandbox) are BOTH Stage::Removed, default false (features/src/lib.rs:1069-1079)

safety.name: sandbox-violation-classification
safety.what: A denied command is turned back into structured evidence rather than an opaque failure. `classify_filesystem_sandbox_violation` only considers a non-zero exit, maps the backend from the sandbox type, and first tries keyword matching over stderr/stdout/aggregated output against seven ordered `(reason, needle)` pairs (operation not permitted, permission denied, read-only file system, seccomp, sandbox, landlock, failed to write file). A curated quick-reject list of well-known non-sandbox shell exit codes is excluded before the last heuristic: on Linux, exit code 128+SIGSYS is classified as a syscall-signal violation. The denied path is extracted from the output text by matching the three colon-prefixed reason markers and accepting only absolute or ./ ../ prefixed candidates, and the snippet is capped. Network denials take a separate path built from the managed proxy's `BlockedRequest`.
invariants: Exit codes 2, 126 and 127 must be rejected as non-sandbox failures before any denial is reported, or ordinary shell misuse would be misclassified (sandboxing/src/violation.rs:33-37, :157-159).
Exit code 0 must never produce a violation (sandboxing/src/violation.rs:138-140).
Extracted paths must be absolute or explicitly relative; a bare word must not be reported as a denied path (sandboxing/src/violation.rs:275-280).

model.name: provider-registry-resolution-chain
model.what: Provider resolution starts from a built-in registry (`built_in_model_providers`) containing openai, amazon-bedrock, amazon-bedrock-runtime, ollama and lmstudio, into which config-declared `model_providers` entries are merged: non-bedrock keys only insert when absent, while bedrock keys may override only base_url/auth/aws/http_headers and any other non-default field is a hard error. Config then selects `model_provider` (defaulting to `openai`) out of the merged map and `create_model_provider` dispatches either to the Amazon Bedrock runtime provider or to the generic `ConfiguredModelProvider`.
invariants: Built-in providers must not be silently overridable by user config except for the explicitly allowed Bedrock fields.
An unknown or removed provider id (e.g. `ollama-chat`) must fail config load with a targeted message rather than falling back to a default.
constants: ChatGPT auth base URL = https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex; API-key base URL = https://api.openai.com/v1

model.name: provider-credential-resolution-chain
model.what: Per-request auth is resolved as an ordered chain: a provider `env_key` API key, then `experimental_bearer_token`, then command-backed auth (an `AuthManager::external_bearer_only` that shells out and caches the token with an optional refresh interval), otherwise the managed CodexAuth snapshot — or an unauthenticated provider when `requires_openai_auth` is false. Amazon Bedrock has its own ladder (command bearer -> managed Bedrock API key -> `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK` -> env AWS credentials -> AWS SDK chain) and its SDK path signs each request with SigV4 over the concrete method, URL, headers and body.
invariants: Conflict validation must reject a provider that sets `aws` together with env_key/experimental_bearer_token/auth/requires_openai_auth.
First-party providers must attach auth headers from the current auth-manager snapshot, and an account switch must not reuse a snapshot keyed to the previous account.
constants: AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK env var name; SigV4 settings = SigningSettings::default()

model.name: remote-model-catalog-with-cache-and-bundled-fallback
model.what: Model discovery fetches the provider's OpenAI-compatible `/models` endpoint under a 5s timeout with provider-resolved auth and route-aware transport, capturing an ETag. Results are written to `$CODEX_HOME/models_cache.json` with a 300s TTL and are only reused when the cached `client_version` matches the current whole-version string; when the endpoint confirms the cached ETag is still current the TTL is merely renewed instead of refetching. If the catalog is absent or unusable the manager keeps the bundled `models.json` compiled into the crate, and a remote catalog replaces it wholesale only when it contains at least one `List`-visible model and the user has ChatGPT account auth, otherwise it is merged by slug.
invariants: Cache entries must be rejected when absent, stale, or for a different client version.
Cache write failures and refresh failures must never fail model discovery — the bundled catalog remains the floor.
constants: Feature::RemoteModels (key remote_models) is Stage::Removed, default false (features/src/lib.rs:1081-1083)

model.name: reasoning-effort-and-context-metadata-translation
model.what: `ReasoningEffort` is an open string enum (none/minimal/low/medium/high/xhigh/max/ultra plus `Custom`) whose `as_str` is the exact wire value, and unknown non-empty strings deserialize into `Custom` so a newer backend value still round-trips. When building a request, `Ultra` is normalized to `Max`, an unset effort falls back to the model's `default_reasoning_level`, `reasoning.summary` is only sent when the model advertises `supports_reasoning_summary_parameter`, and `reasoning.context` is set to all-turns only for Responses-Lite models; all of this lands in the serialized `reasoning` object. Context metadata is likewise derived from the catalogue: `resolved_context_window` prefers `context_window` and falls back to `max_context_window`, and `auto_compact_token_limit` clamps a configured limit to 90% of that window.
invariants: `as_str` must remain the single source of the wire value — serialization must never diverge from parsing.
An empty reasoning effort string must be an error, but any other unknown non-empty value must be accepted as Custom rather than rejected.

model.name: chatgpt-oauth-pkce-loopback-login
model.what: Interactive login spins up a short-lived loopback HTTP server on port 1455 (falling back to 1457) that builds an authorize URL against https://auth.openai.com with a fresh S256 PKCE verifier/challenge and a random `state`, then validates the `/auth/callback` `state` before accepting the code and exchanging it for tokens. Headless environments have a separate device-code path, and the refresh-token authority endpoint can be redirected for testing.
invariants: The callback `state` must be validated before the authorization code is used; a mismatch returns HTTP 400 and no token exchange occurs.
The PKCE verifier must be 64 random bytes encoded URL-safe without padding, with the challenge being its SHA-256.
constants: PKCE verifier entropy = 64 bytes; callback channel capacity = 16

model.name: auth-persistence-backend-and-unauthorized-recovery
model.what: Credentials are persisted through a pluggable `AuthStorageBackend`: a plain `auth.json` written 0600, an OS keyring entry under service 'Codex Auth' keyed by a hash of CODEX_HOME, or an encrypted secrets-manager store (with the plaintext file deleted on successful write). Token lifetime is policed by a proactive refresh window and an `UnauthorizedRecovery` state machine that, on a 401, first performs a guarded reload that only applies when the on-disk account id still matches, then refreshes from the authority, distinguishing permanent refresh-token failures (expired/reused/revoked/account-mismatch) from transient IO errors.
invariants: A reload must be skipped when the account id on disk differs from the expected one, so another account's tokens are never adopted.
A permanent refresh failure must not be retried as if it were transient.
constants: auth.json mode = 0o600; KEYRING_SERVICE = 'Codex Auth'; REFRESH_TOKEN_URL = https://auth.openai.com/oauth/token

model.name: responses-websocket-transport-with-https-fallback
model.what: When the active provider advertises `supports_websockets`, the client uses a persistent Responses-over-WebSocket transport with a prewarm `response.create` (generate=false) as the first connection attempt for a turn and a cached session reused across requests. WebSocket use is a per-session one-way latch: once the retry budget is exhausted the client flips `disable_websockets` and every later request goes over HTTPS, emitting a warning event and a `codex.transport.fallback_to_http` counter. Unbounded connection retries are a separate, default-on path that keeps retrying connection failures with doubling delay for non-internal, non-Bedrock sampling turns.
invariants: The WebSocket-to-HTTP fallback must be irreversible for the session (an AtomicBool swap, never reset).
Fallback must only trigger after the retry budget is exhausted, and the cached websocket session must be discarded when it does.

extension.name: hook-lifecycle-event-engine
extension.what: A Claude-Code-compatible lifecycle hook engine (`ClaudeHooksEngine`) dispatches 11 named events (PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, Stop) to command or MCP-tool handlers selected by exact/pipe/regex matchers. Per-event parsing converts handler stdout/stderr/exit code into control effects: PreToolUse can block a tool call or rewrite `updated_input`, PermissionRequest can allow/deny an approval, PostToolUse can block a tool result and inject model feedback, UserPromptSubmit can stop a turn, Stop can force continuation. Effects land in the agent loop at the PreToolUse gate in the tool registry, the turn-stop path in the session loop and the approval path.
invariants: Only an explicit blocking signal produces a control effect: decision:block with a non-empty reason, permissionDecision:deny with a non-empty reason, continue:false, or exit code 2 with non-empty stderr (hooks/src/events/pre_tool_use.rs:241-277).
A block needs a non-empty reason; an empty/missing reason downgrades the run to Failed instead of blocking (hooks/src/engine/output_parser.rs:210-220).
Stop aggregation gives should_stop precedence over should_block (hooks/src/events/stop.rs:367).
constants: Default command-hook timeout 600s with a 1s minimum (hooks/src/engine/discovery.rs:728)
11 hook events, 9 of which honour matchers (hooks/src/lib.rs:23-52)

extension.name: hook-mode-gating-and-output-spill
extension.what: Every handler's execution mode is derived from its kind: only command hooks with `async=true` are `HookExecutionMode::Async`, and `can_apply_control_effects()` is exactly `execution_mode() == Sync`, so an async handler can never block, deny, stop or rewrite. Async completions are drained at turn boundaries and re-filtered so only Context/Warning/Error entries survive; only synchronous runs emit HookStarted/HookCompleted. Handler `additionalContext` is parsed into strict deny-unknown-fields wire structs, appended as developer-role `HookAdditionalContext` fragments, and oversized text passes through a `HookOutputSpiller` that writes the full body to a temp spill directory and substitutes a truncated form.
invariants: `can_apply_control_effects()` is exactly `execution_mode() == Sync`; no async handler may block, deny, stop or rewrite input (hooks/src/engine/mod.rs:96-99).
MCP-tool hooks are always Sync (hooks/src/engine/mod.rs:88-94).
`additionalContextLimit` is honoured only for PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit and SubagentStart; other events warn and drop it (hooks/src/engine/discovery.rs:536-553).
constants: Spill directory 'hook_outputs' under the OS temp dir, per thread id (hooks/src/output_spill.rs:11, :45-51)

extension.name: hook-trust-ledger
extension.what: Hook discovery walks the config layer stack low-to-high plus managed requirements plus plugin hook sources, normalizes each handler, and computes a `hook_hash` over a normalized TOML identity rather than the raw source text. That hash is compared against the persisted `hooks.state.<key>.trusted_hash` to derive `HookTrustStatus::{Managed,Trusted,Modified,Untrusted}`; only enabled handlers whose status is Managed or Trusted (or whose source carries `bypass_hook_trust`) become live configured handlers. Hook state may only be read from the User and SessionFlags config layers; managed hooks are unconditionally enabled; approval is persisted by writing the trusted hash.
invariants: Persisted hook enable/trust state can only be written by User and SessionFlags layers; project, managed and plugin layers may declare hooks but not write user hook state (hooks/src/config_rules.rs:8-29).
Managed hooks are unconditionally enabled and always Managed status; an enable=false state is ignored for them (hooks/src/engine/discovery.rs:776-789).
Untrusted or Modified hooks are never registered and therefore cannot run unless trust is bypassed (hooks/src/engine/discovery.rs:693-699).
constants: Default trust status with no stored hash is Untrusted (hooks/src/engine/discovery.rs:782)

extension.name: layered-skill-catalog-developer-injection
extension.what: Host skills are discovered from an ordered, layered root set (repo .agents/skills between project root and cwd, Project layer skills/, deprecated $CODEX_HOME/skills, ~/.agents/skills, the embedded .system cache, System layer skills/, plus plugin and extra roots). Merging dedupes on `path_to_skills_md`, drops later duplicates, filters by product restriction and sorts by a fixed scope rank (Repo 0, User 1, System 2, Admin 3). The resulting catalog is rendered as `AvailableSkillsInstructions`, whose fragment role is literally "developer", and reaches the model as prompt text or a world-state fragment — not as a tool call.
invariants: Root/scope precedence is load-bearing: the first snapshot to claim a path wins and later duplicates are dropped rather than merged (ext/skills/src/loader/host_merge.rs:232-269).
The host catalog must reach the model as developer-role prompt text; the skills list/read tools carry only non-host authority (ext/skills/src/tools/mod.rs:63-70).
Rendering must never exceed the resolved metadata budget — over-budget skills are omitted with an omission notice, never silently dropped.

extension.name: explicit-mention-and-implicit-skill-invocation
extension.what: Explicit selection is input-driven: structured `UserInput::Skill`/`Mention` with a skill path resolve by canonical or discovery path, and text inputs are scanned for `$name` tokens using `TOOL_MENTION_SIGIL = '$'` with common environment-variable names excluded; a plain name matches only when it is unique among enabled skills. Selected skills are injected as `<skill>...</skill>` fragments in the *user* role, byte-truncated with a warning. Implicit invocation is a separate observation-only path: it tokenizes a shell command and recognizes either a script run under a skill's `scripts/` directory or a read of the skill's document, producing analytics and contributor callbacks — it never injects instructions.

extension.name: mcp-client-transport-and-startup-budget
extension.what: Codex-as-MCP-client materializes one of five pending transport variants from a recipe: in-process duplex, stdio server, plain streamable HTTP, streamable HTTP with an OAuth persistor, and streamable HTTP with a stored access token only. Stdio process placement is abstracted behind a `StdioServerLauncher` trait (local child of the orchestrator versus executor-managed). A per-session protocol mode selects the rmcp lifecycle: Legacy uses 2025-06-18 with explicit `Initialize`; the 2026-07-28 mode prefers the newer version with legacy fallback and, for stdio, additionally requires the server config to set `CODEX_MCP_PROTOCOL_VERSION=2026-07-28`. Session recovery must go through a single-permit semaphore and re-check that the failed service is still current before replacing it (rmcp-client/src/rmcp_client.rs:395, :1410-1434).

OPTIONAL_MCP_STARTUP_GRACE = 1 s before optional servers are omitted from the catalog (codex-mcp/src/connection_manager/tool_catalog.rs:35)

extension.name: mcp-tool-catalog-exposure-and-elicitation-roundtrip
extension.what: The catalog aggregates every enabled server's tools into one model-facing list: listing is paginated with caps on pages, total items and cursor size, rejects repeated cursors and wraps the loop in an overall timeout; per-server definitions are cached in a process-wide LRU keyed by a catalog identity fingerprint with a TTL and monotonically increasing fetch tickets so only the newest accepted fetch publishes. Published snapshots always strip tool annotations because annotations drive approval and parallelism decisions. Separately, server-initiated elicitation is routed to the user and back: the elicitation service intercepts `ElicitRequest` plus custom `elicitation/create` and `openai/form` methods, applies a policy (auto-decline, strict auto-review, auto-accept only for empty-property forms), and otherwise emits an `EventMsg::ElicitationRequest` with a Codex-generated id while pausing the tool-call inactivity timeout by reference count.

The elicitation id must be Codex-generated, not copied from the MCP connection, so separate runtimes can reuse the same server request id without colliding.
The operation timeout must not be charged while an elicitation is pending — pause is reference-counted and only active time is subtracted (rmcp-client/src/rmcp_client.rs:189-257).

extension.name: plugin-manifest-and-marketplace-distribution
extension.what: A plugin is a directory with a manifest that contributes four capability kinds — skills, mcp_servers, hooks (inline list or paths), and an interface block with a capability list. The plugins manager resolves configured marketplaces (local / git / npm sources with ref, sha and registry scoping) and installs plugins, returning an install outcome with plugin id, version, installed path and auth policy plus a detail record enumerating the plugin's skills, hooks, apps and MCP server names. Plugin-sourced hooks are resolved into the hook engine for a given config layer stack, gated on `config.plugins_enabled`. Installation and authentication policy are separate enums (install: not-available / available / installed-by-default; auth: on-install / on-use).

extension.name: code-mode-javascript-host

The host is a separate process chosen by the thread manager (`ProcessOwnedCodeModeSessionProvider` versus `DisabledCodeModeSessionProvider`), and remote code-mode host transports (WebSocket/gRPC) are rejected at app-server startup when the host feature is disabled.

extension.what: Collaboration modes are prompt-and-tool policy bundles rather than database state: a mode is presented as a mask of mode + model + reasoning effort + developer instructions, the Plan preset supplies a template as developer instructions with medium effort, and the resulting mode is injected as a role=developer fragment wrapped in `<collaboration_mode>` inside world state (so it participates in the world-state hash/diff machinery). In Plan mode the `update_plan` tool is refused outright with 'update_plan is a TODO/checklist tool and is not allowed in Plan mode', and plan contents surface as `EventMsg::PlanUpdate` rather than a persisted file. `Feature::CollaborationModes` is `Stage::Removed` with `default_enabled: true` (features/src/lib.rs:1432-1437), so the flag no longer gates anything; the templates crate still participates through world state.

Mode instructions must carry role=developer, not user, so they are treated as system-level direction (core/src/context/world_state/collaboration_mode.rs:122-143).

extension.name: extension-registry-contributor-seams
extension.what: Extensions plug into Core through a typed contributor registry rather than ad-hoc hooks: `ExtensionRegistry` holds twelve contributor vectors (thread lifecycle, turn lifecycle, config, token usage, skill invocation, approval review, context, MCP server, turn input, tool, tool lifecycle, turn item) which Core dispatches in registration order from `Session::emit_*_lifecycle` loops. Extension state is keyed by concrete `TypeId` via insert/get-or-init, and the built registry is immutable — only the builder accepts contributors. A no-op event sink is used when no host sink is installed, so an extension can be loaded in a context that has no client attached. Extensions shipped as first-party crates in this tree include agent, connectors, git-attribution, goal, guardian-v2, image-generation, items, mcp, memories, queue, skills and web-search.
invariants: The built `ExtensionRegistry` is immutable; contributors may only be added through the builder (ext/extension-api/src/registry.rs:27-84).
Extension state must be keyed by concrete `TypeId`, not by a string name, so two extensions cannot collide.
Contributor dispatch order is registration order and is load-bearing — a turn-lifecycle contributor must not assume another ran first.
